title: We’ve been testing the same crypto trading bot since March. The biggest lesson wasn’t the return — it was drawdown.
author: profittoinvest
selftext:
We started testing our crypto trading system in March 2026.

This is not an AI “predict the next candle” experiment. We’re treating the bot more like an engineering system: test, run LIVE, compare, find where it breaks, and iterate.

Since then, the strategy has gone through a lot of changes, and probably the biggest lesson has been that improving a bot is much less about finding a “perfect entry” and much more about understanding how the **entire open portfolio behaves over time**.

The current configuration has been running since July under fixed rules, so we can finally collect clean LIVE data and compare it with standardized backtests.

Before that, we were constantly experimenting.

One of our earlier configurations used a take-profit allocation of roughly:

**TP1 40% / TP2 40% / TP3 20%**

On paper it looked reasonable.

In practice, it was slowly killing the upside of the strategy.

After a lot of testing, we found that the system performed much better when most of the position was allowed to remain open for the larger move.

The current structure is:

**TP1 5% / TP2 5% / TP3 90%**

That change turned out to be much more important than we originally expected.

# The difficult part was drawdown

The worst period in our earlier testing came around late May / early June.

The system experienced a drawdown of more than **47%**.

It remained profitable overall and eventually recovered, but that period forced us to rethink how we were looking at risk.

We stopped treating every signal as an isolated trade.

Instead, we started looking at the **entire open portfolio as one system**.

That changed a lot.

Old positions can accumulate.

Capital gets locked.

Long or short exposure can become heavily skewed.

A strategy can look healthy trade-by-trade while the portfolio underneath is becoming increasingly fragile.

So we started building portfolio-level controls around that behaviour.

At certain moments we cut accumulated old positions, control directional imbalance and try to prevent the portfolio from becoming overloaded with too many LONGs or SHORTs on one side.

# Then we pushed the backtests further back

We ran the system through historical data going back to 2020.

That exposed another problem.

There were periods where old positions accumulated for too long and caused very sharp equity drawdowns.

After another round of changes, backtests and fixes, we managed to reduce those events substantially.

But we still haven't found a configuration that completely eliminates deep drawdowns without damaging the edge.

In longer simulations, we still see periods of roughly **45–50% peak-to-trough drawdown**.

And that is something we have simply decided not to hide.

Sometimes the situation looks especially bad from a free-capital perspective because a significant amount of capital is tied up in open positions, many of which later recover.

But from an equity-risk perspective, drawdown is still drawdown and has to be treated as such.

# The current configuration has been tracked cleanly since July

From **July 4 to September 30**, the standardized backtest returned approximately:

**+151%**

The LIVE account over the same period returned approximately:

**+109%**

So there is a difference of more than **40 percentage points** between simulation and LIVE execution.

That gap is now one of the most interesting parts of the project.

We are currently breaking both histories down and looking for exactly where the paths began to diverge.

Some likely causes are already fairly clear: the system can generate more signals than the available capital can accept, LIVE margin availability changes the sequence of accepted trades, some portfolio-protection rules still require manual intervention, and real execution introduces timing, fill and fee differences that an idealized backtest cannot reproduce perfectly.

The important part for us is not pretending that the backtest is reality.

It isn't.

The useful question is:

**Why did LIVE and simulation diverge, and can we model that divergence better?**

# Position sizing turned out to matter a lot too

Our current simulations suggest that around **4% of account capital per position** gives a good balance for this particular system.

But we do not continuously recalculate 4% after every trade.

Instead, at the **beginning of each month** we calculate approximately 4% of the account value and use that as the base position size.

Depending on how much excess free capital is available, we may apply an additional planned increase at that point.

Once the monthly stake is set, however, it remains a **fixed nominal amount for the entire month**.

Then at the beginning of the next month we recalculate it again.

We found this more practical than constantly resizing every trade as equity moves, and it also makes LIVE behaviour easier to compare with backtests.

Interestingly, even if the nominal stake is gradually increased over time, its effective percentage of total equity can still decline as the account grows faster than the stake.

That leaves more free margin available for future signals.

We are still testing where the best balance sits.

# One experiment surprised us

We completely reversed the take-profit allocation.

Same entry logic.

Same period.

Same leverage.

Same initial capital.

Original:

**5 / 5 / 90 → +151.3%, max DD 27.7%**

Reversed:

**90 / 5 / 5 → +84.4%, max DD 41.2%**

So even after radically changing how profits were realized, the strategy remained profitable over the same 89-day period.

But taking most of the profit early produced both **lower return and higher drawdown**.

That was probably one of the clearest reminders that a high TP hit rate or early profit-taking does not necessarily mean lower risk.

The entry system alone is not the whole edge.

The distribution of exits matters enormously.

# What we are still trying to solve

The same problem we have been working on for months:

**How do you reduce drawdown without destroying the part of the strategy that actually generates the edge?**

Every time we make the system “safer”, there is a risk of cutting off the trades that pay for everything else.

So for now, the process remains pretty simple:

**test → run LIVE → compare → find divergence → fix → test again**

No magic indicator.

No perfect backtest.

Just a lot of iteration.

And after several months of doing this, I’m increasingly convinced that the hardest part of building a trading bot is not finding entries.

It is controlling what happens **after dozens of entries start interacting with each other inside the same portfolio**.

I’m curious how others approach this.

**What portfolio-level controls have actually helped you reduce drawdown without killing expectancy?**

*Backtested performance is simulated and does not represent actual account performance. Cryptocurrency trading involves significant risk and past performance does not guarantee future results.*

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Showing the 45% to 50% drawdowns and the gap between live and backtest is what makes this useful. One caution on the 5/5/90 versus 90/5/5 result: 89 days is one regime, and letting winners run tends to win in strong trends and lose in chop, so I'd check the same comparison on other periods before concluding. For the live gap, tagging each missed or reordered trade by cause (margin, timing, fees) would show which part is fixable. Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for macro releases) is one source you could use to see whether the deepest drawdowns cluster around news.

replies.author: profittoinvest
replies.body:
Thanks — and that’s a fair caution.

We actually have another period that behaved very differently: roughly **March to early July**, which was much more bearish/choppy than the July–September window.

On that period, the **5/5/90** configuration returned around **+42%**, while the **90/5/5** version made only about **+5%**.

So the difference between the two TP structures also appeared in a very different market regime, which makes the result more interesting to us.

That said, we **don’t have reliable LIVE data from that earlier period** because we were still changing settings and experimenting heavily at the time. For that window, we only trust the backtests.

Since July, the rules have been much more stable, which is why the current LIVE vs backtest comparison is far more useful.

And yes — the trade-by-trade reconciliation you mentioned is exactly what we’re working on now. Thanks for the feedback.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: That's useful, thanks. A second regime where the same ordering held makes the result more convincing, even if it's backtest only for that window. Good luck with the reconciliation.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: drawdown being the real lesson tracks. moving the exit target can make the headline line look better while the open book quietly carries far more at once, and you only find out when a few positions go wrong together. freezing the config in july was the right move, clean live data under one rule set beats the whole experimental stretch before it.

replies.author: profittoinvest
replies.body:
Exactly. Freezing the configuration in July was probably the turning point for us.

Before that, every improvement also moved the reference point, so comparing LIVE with backtest was much less useful.

Now, when the paths diverge, we can actually investigate specific causes — missed signals, margin availability, timing, fees, manual portfolio controls, etc.

And your point about the open book is exactly why we stopped looking at trades one by one. A portfolio can look fine at trade level while quietly accumulating a lot of correlated risk underneath.

It’s also worth noting that the results have been much stronger in the more recent period. Our backtests suggest the bot performs better during sustained uptrends, partly because the system tends to generate and maintain more LONG exposure in that environment.

That doesn’t mean an uptrend automatically guarantees better results, but so far the regime clearly seems to matter.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: yeah, once the reference stops moving a divergence turns into a list of suspects instead of a shrug. margin and missed signals are usually where it lives. same reason my own paper desk, Quantradin, locks the rules before the first fill. I built it for stocks and options though, so no help on crypto. free, quantradin.com if you want to compare.

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body: That 5/5/90 vs 40/40/20 flip is the whole game. Letting one winner run beats scalping three TPs, but only in a trending regime. The 47% drawdown is the real story, not the return.

replies.author: profittoinvest
replies.body:
I agree that the drawdown is the more important part.

The interesting thing is that the 5/5/90 advantage also appeared in a very different regime. From roughly March to early July, which was much more bearish/choppy, the 5/5/90 backtest returned around +42%, while 90/5/5 made only about +5%.

So at least in our tests, it doesn’t seem to be only a “trending market” effect.

That said, we only have reliable LIVE validation from July onward, so I wouldn’t treat the earlier period as proof.

And yes — reducing that 45–50% drawdown without killing expectancy is probably the biggest problem we’re trying to solve now.
